chapters.title: Chapter 4: Beyond Percentages: Control, Rights and Exits

lessons.title: Why Owning 51 Percent Is Not Control: Resolutions, Board Seats and Reserved Matters

children.text: Two founders, same week. One holds 55% of her company and cannot approve her own annual budget without an investor's written consent. The other holds 21% and decides almost everything that matters. Neither situation is unusual, and neither can be explained by the cap table alone. Control in an Indian private company comes from three separate places, and the shareholding percentage is only the first of them.

body.text: Ownership, votes and control are three different things. Your percentage decides your share of the money. The Companies Act decides what a vote can do. The shareholders' agreement decides what you are allowed to do at all.

children.text: Layer One: What a Shareholder Vote Can Do

markDefs.definition: A shareholder resolution that requires the votes cast in favour to be at least three times the votes cast against, which in practice means a 75% threshold. Used for the most significant corporate decisions.

children.text: The Companies Act, 2013 sorts shareholder decisions into two buckets. An ordinary resolution needs more votes for than against, which is a simple majority of the votes cast. A
needs votes in favour of at least three times the votes against. Which bucket a decision falls into is fixed by law, not by your agreement.

cells: Whoever controls more than half the votes controls the board over time
Routine, but it still needs a majority
Covered in Lesson 1.2, alongside Form SH-7
Anyone holding more than 25% can block a change to the company's constitution
Amending the memorandum, including the objects clause
Changing what business you are in needs 75% support
Issuing shares to new investors by preferential allotment
Every priced round depends on this passing
Reducing share capital or a large buyback
Returning capital to shareholders is never a simple majority decision

body.label: The number that matters most
body.context: A holder with more than a quarter of the votes can defeat any special resolution, which includes amending the articles and issuing shares to a new investor. You do not need a majority to hold real power. You need a blocking stake.

children.text: Voting Power Is Not the Same as Ownership

Options do not vote until they are exercised. That single fact separates the economic cap table from the voting register. TiffinBox after its Series A has 28,057 fully diluted shares, but 4,209 of those are unexercised options, leaving 23,848 shares that actually carry votes. Preference shares are assumed here to vote on an as-converted basis, as most Indian shareholders' agreements provide.

body.caption: TiffinBox after the Series A: economic ownership vs voting power

children.text: Read the last column carefully. The founders hold 41.93% of the votes, so they cannot pass an ordinary resolution on their own. The seed fund and the Series A investor together hold 50.38%, so they can. And the Series A investor alone holds 29.41%, comfortably above the 25% needed to block any special resolution, which means no future round can be approved without them.

body.title: Voting power at TiffinBox after the Series A (% of 23,848 voting shares)

children.text: Layer Two: The Board Runs the Company

Shareholders meet a few times a year. The board meets often and exercises most of the company's powers, from approving borrowings and investments to appointing key managerial personnel. Board seats are negotiated in the shareholders' agreement and usually have nothing to do with exact percentages. A 20% investor commonly gets one seat of five.

body.caption: Who actually controls a five-member board

cells: Founders carry ordinary board decisions, subject to reserved matters
The independent director decides every contested vote, so who appoints them matters enormously
Founders can be outvoted on operational matters even while holding more equity
Founder majority with an investor veto list
Board control is real but bounded: anything on the reserved matters list still needs investor consent

body.text: When a shareholders' agreement provides for an independent or nominee director appointed by mutual agreement, treat that clause as seriously as the equity split. On a two-two board, that one person decides every deadlock. Agree the selection process, the term and what happens if the seat falls vacant, before you need any of it.

children.text: Layer Three: Reserved Matters, Where Control Really Lives

markDefs.definition: A list of decisions in the shareholders' agreement that cannot be taken without the affirmative consent of specified investors, regardless of how the shareholder or board vote goes.

children.text: Most founder frustration comes from neither of the first two layers. It comes from the

list, sometimes called affirmative vote rights or veto rights. These are contractual, they are written into the shareholders' agreement and mirrored in the articles of association, and they operate whatever your percentage says.

body.caption: Common reserved matters, and how hard to push back

cells: Issuing new shares or changing share capital
Protects them from being diluted on bad terms
Selling the company or a material asset
Protects the value of their investment
Reasonable, though watch how "material" is defined
Changing the nature of the business
Reasonable, but keep the wording narrow so normal product evolution is not caught
Fine, but negotiate a realistic threshold that grows with revenue
Push for a deemed-approval mechanism if no objection is raised within a set period
Hiring senior staff or setting their compensation
Push back hard. This slows down hiring in a market where speed decides outcomes
Changing the ESOP plan or pool
Reasonable, but ask for headroom to make ordinary grants without a fresh consent each time
Guards against value leaking to founders' other interests

body.text: Watch for two things in the reserved matters clause. First, whether consent is needed from each investor separately or from an investor majority. Separate vetoes mean a small shareholder from an old round can hold up a deal years later. Second, whether the rights survive as the investor's stake falls. Ask for a threshold below which the veto rights fall away, for example if the investor drops below 10%.

columns.label: What the law gives you
points: More than 50% of votes carries ordinary resolutions
More than 25% blocks any special resolution
Minority shareholders have statutory remedies against oppression and mismanagement

columns.label: What the contract gives away
points: Reserved matters requiring investor consent whatever the vote
Information rights, budgets and reporting obligations
Drag-along rights that can force you into a sale

body.title: Can the Series A investor block you?
body.prompt: TiffinBox has 23,848 voting shares after the Series A. The Series A investor holds 7,014 of them. What percentage of the votes is that? Answer to two decimal places.
body.explanation: 7,014 ÷ 23,848 = 29.41%. That is comfortably above 25%, so this investor alone can defeat any special resolution, including the preferential allotment needed to close your next round. Their 25.00% economic stake understates their power.

body.title: Which resolution do you need?
body.question: You want to amend your articles of association to add new transfer restrictions. Founders hold 41.93% of the votes, the seed fund 20.97% and the Series A investor 29.41%. Who must agree?
options: Only the founders, because they are the largest single block
The founders and the seed fund, because together they cross 50%
Enough shareholders to reach the special resolution threshold, which means the founders plus at least one major investor, and the Series A investor alone can block it
Nobody, because articles can be amended by a board resolution
body.explanation: Amending the articles needs a special resolution. Founders at 41.93% are far short on their own. Founders plus the seed fund reach 62.90%, which is still short. And with 29.41%, the Series A investor can defeat the resolution whatever anyone else does.

body.title: Name the veto list
body.textWithBlank: The list of decisions in a shareholders' agreement that need investor consent regardless of the shareholder vote is called the ___ matters list.
body.explanation: Reserved matters, also called affirmative vote rights or veto rights, are contractual. They are the layer of control that has nothing to do with your percentage.

body.title: The hire you cannot make
body.scenario: You hold 38% of your Bengaluru SaaS company and chair a five-member board with three founder-appointed seats. A competitor is shutting down and you can hire its four-person engineering team this week, at a total cost of ₹1.6 crore a year, which is 18% above your approved budget line for engineering. Your shareholders' agreement reserves both "any deviation from the approved annual budget exceeding 10% of any line item" and "appointment of any employee with annual compensation above ₹50 lakh" to the consent of each investor holding 5% or more. There are four such investors, one of whom is travelling and slow to respond.
body.prompt: What can you do now, and what should you fix in the agreement?
body.modelAnswer:
What you can do now:
1. Accept that board control does not help here. Your three seats carry ordinary board decisions, but reserved matters sit above the board. Proceeding without consent would breach the agreement and could trigger a default clause.
2. Get consent quickly rather than perfectly. Send one short written request covering both reserved matters together, with the commercial rationale, the cost, and a deadline. Most investors respond to a clear ask with a date on it.
3. Look for a lawful structure that does not trigger the clause. Can two of the four join now within the existing budget line and compensation threshold, with the rest joining next quarter after a budget revision? Structure it honestly, not as a device to dodge consent.
4. Escalate through your board's investor directors. They can chase their own colleagues faster than you can.

What to fix at the next round:
1. Change consent from each investor to an investor majority, defined by shareholding. This alone removes most of the delay risk.
2. Add a deemed-consent mechanism: if no written objection arrives within, say, seven business days of a complete request, consent is deemed given.
3. Raise the thresholds and index them. A ₹50 lakh compensation trigger set at seed stage is meaningless by Series B, and a 10% line item deviation is far too tight for a growing company.
4. Add a falling-away threshold, so veto rights lapse for any investor whose stake drops below an agreed level.
5. Carve out ordinary-course hiring within an agreed headcount plan, so the board approves the plan once rather than each hire individually.

body.title: Auditing your own control
steps: Separate your cap table into economic ownership and voting shares, leaving unexercised options out of the voting column.
Calculate where you and each investor sit against 50% and 25% of the votes.
List who can block a special resolution on their own, since every future round depends on one.
Write down the current board composition and how each seat is appointed and removed.
Read the reserved matters list end to end and mark each one as reasonable, negotiable or unacceptable.
Check whether consent is per investor or by investor majority, and whether rights fall away below a shareholding threshold.
Confirm the same provisions appear in the articles of association, not only in the shareholders' agreement.
Re-run this audit after every round, because thresholds move as you are diluted.

cards.definition: A shareholder resolution carried when votes in favour exceed votes against, a simple majority of votes cast.
A resolution needing votes in favour of at least three times the votes against, effectively 75%.
More than 25% of votes, enough to defeat any special resolution.
Decisions that require specified investors' consent regardless of the shareholder or board vote.
Another name for a reserved matter veto held by an investor.
A director appointed to the board by a particular shareholder under the shareholders' agreement.
A clause treating consent as given if no objection is received within an agreed period.

points: Control sits in three layers: shareholder votes, the board, and contractual reserved matters.
Ordinary resolutions need a simple majority of votes cast, special resolutions need votes in favour of at least three times the votes against.
More than 25% of the votes is a blocking stake, and every priced round needs a special resolution to pass.
Unexercised options do not vote, so voting percentages differ from fully diluted ownership. At TiffinBox the founders hold 35.64% economically but 41.93% of the votes.
Board seats are negotiated, not proportional, and on a balanced board the independent director decides everything contested.
Reserved matters are where most founder frustration lives, because they operate whatever your percentage is.
Negotiate investor-majority consent instead of per-investor vetoes, deemed consent after a deadline, realistic thresholds, and rights that fall away as a stake shrinks.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not legal, tax or investment advice. TiffinBox Foods and the other companies and people described are fictional, and all share counts and percentages are illustrative. Resolution requirements, the treatment of preference shareholders' voting rights, minority shareholder remedies and the exemptions available to private companies are governed by the Companies Act, 2013 and its rules, which change over time, and the voting arrangements in any company depend on its articles of association and shareholders' agreement. Consult a qualified company secretary or lawyer before relying on any governance position.
